Freudian Concepts in the Twenty-First Century: A Neuropsychoanalytic Update and Discussion

Jane Abrams , Ross Balchin , Iftah Biran , Rudi Coetzer , Daniela Mosri , Jose Fernando Zúñiga and David Olds

David Olds

http://orcid.org/0000-0001-5205-4586

http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3126-8344

http://orcid.org/0000-0002-4209-4098

David Olds  

After a rich collection of articles was published in our 25th volume, we are now ready to start volume 26 with an equally interesting set of papers on topics that focus on the core of neuropsychoanalysis, such as Freudian concepts and clinical work. As old as Freud’s theory is, it is still difficult to find the complexity and quality that his model of the mind offers anywhere else. Updating and discussing some of its core notions is a crucial task of neuropsychoanalysis. The exploration of Freudian concepts, such as primary and secondary processes and the perceptual-conscious system, from a neuropsychoanalytic perspective contribute to our further understanding of Freud’s ideas in the twenty-first century. No less important is our commitment to support the development of the clinical implications of neuropsychoanalysis by presenting a clinical paper that shows the outcome of looking at a case from an integrative point of view to deeply understand the challenges of neurodiversity to our usual techniques. For the target article section, we present Doug Watt’s elaborate response to the commentaries on his recent paper “The Separation Distress Hypothesis of Depression - An Update and Systematic Review” (Watt, 2023), which had commentaries by Paul Badcock and Karl Friston (Badcock & Friston, 2023), Barton Blinder (Blinder, 2023), Otto Kernberg (Kernberg, 2023), Ken Davis and Christian Montag (Davis & Montag, 2023), Stephen Siviy (Siviy, 2023), and Howard Steele (Steele, 2023). Watt’s careful response to each author could be considered another target article due to his thorough elaboration on several topics that will inform the reader interested in depression about further clarifications and potential lines of research. Relevant work from our vibrant neuropsychoanalytic community also contributes to this issue. We report on the research presented at the 22nd Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society, which particularly addressed the topic of PLAY. Our Book Review and Research Digest sections bring us up to date with recent work related to neuropsychoanalysis.

Raheleh Jafari  

Time perception, the unconscious, working memory, the Pcpt-Cs. system

In this article, we explore the Pcpt-Cs. (perceptual-consciousness) system in Freud’s work and its relation to the subject of time perception, as well as its study from a neuroscience perspective. According to Freud, the Pcpt-Cs. system is a porous system located at the front of the psychic apparatus, on the border of the external and internal worlds. We first offer an overview of the Pcpt-Cs. system in Freud's papers throughout different years of his career. In this regard, we note that Freud considers our perception of time to be the result of a continuous and discontinuous connection between the unconscious and the external world through the Pcpt-Cs. system. In the second part, we review new studies concerning time perception in neuroscience. We suggest that we cannot locate a particular system characterized by the features that Freud attributed to the Pcpt-Cs. system in the brain. Nevertheless, if we are to point out the most similar part of the brain to the Pcpt-Cs. system based on what we have investigated throughout the present article, the systems involved in working memory would be our best suggestion.

<aut authindexid="Maroun, Mouna" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Mouna</nfirst> <nlast>Maroun</nlast> <nbio>Studied Psychology in Haifa and obtained her Ph.D. in Psychobiology. She continued for a postdoc in Paris in Neuroscience and is now a Professor in the University of Haifa. She is interested in the interaction between the prefrontal cortex and the amygdala and how this interaction is modified following stress. In recent years, she focused her study to address possible differences in these mechanisms between adult and juvenile rats. Maroun recently started also addressing the effects of unhealthy diet on the juvenile brain and her findings support the vulnerability of the juvenile developing brain.</nbio></aut>
<aut authindexid="Shamay-Tsoory, Simone" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Simone</nfirst> <nlast>Shamay-Tsoory</nlast> <ndeg dgr="PHD"/> <nbio>Professor of Psychology at the University of Haifa. She serves as the head of the Social and Affective Neuroscience Lab and the newly established Brain and Behavior Hub. As a social neuroscientist, Professor Shamay-Tsoory's research focuses on understanding how the brain processes social cognition and emotional experiences. To explore these topics, she utilizes advanced neuroscience techniques such as neuroimaging, neurostimulation, and psychopharmacology. Her investigations involve both typically developing individuals and those with autism spectrum conditions (ASC). One area of Professor Shamay-Tsoory's work is centered around the neural basis of human empathy. She has explored the dual brain systems involved in empathy, including an emotional contagion system and a cognitive-perceptual system. Through her recent research, she has employed fNIRS-based hyperscanning, which involves scanning the brains of two or more individuals simultaneously. This approach allows her to study the coordination and coupling of brain activity during social interactions.</nbio></aut>
<aut authindexid="Axmacher, Nikolai" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Nikolai</nfirst> <nlast>Axmacher</nlast> <ndeg dgr="PHD"/> <nbio>Studied Philosophy and Medicine in Berlin and Paris and is Professor of Neuropsychology at Ruhr University Bochum. He investigates the neural foundations of memory functions and dysfunctions using cognitive neuroscience methods in humans, with a particular interest in the processing of specific experiences by the brain. He investigates a wide range of memory processes from working to long-term memory and memory consolidation, autobiographical memory and repression, and addresses questions such as: How are experiences represented in the brain and transformed into memory traces? How do these experiences shape, and are shaped by, our Self? And how is memory compromised by trauma, interpsychic conflicts and Alzheimer’s dementia? Axmacher uses a combination of functional MRI at 3T and 7T, simultaneous EEG/fMRI and intracranial EEG recordings. His work has been published in more than 140 articles including papers in Science, Nature Neuroscience, Neuron etc., and was cited more than 13,000 times. Nikolai Axmacher was awarded several prestigious awards, most recently an ERC Consolidator Grant (2M€) in 2019. He is an elected member of the Memory Disorders Research Society and serves on several international research panels.</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A02" authindexid="Asmar, Najla" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Najla</nfirst> <nlast>Asmar</nlast> <nbio>Supervising clinical psychologist, and Chief Psychologist at the English Hospital in Nazareth. Founder and manager of MA’ANA Center at the English Hospital, a center for mental health treatment, evaluation and supervision. Najla Asmar has worked for many years at the Developmental Psychological Treatment Station of the Ministry of Health in Haifa, and is a graduate of the Psychotherapy program and the Experienced Therapists program at the Psychoanalytic Society in Israel.</nbio></aut>

<aut affid="A05" authindexid="Shalev, Idit" listed="true" role="author"><npreti oldnpreti="Dr." type="TITLE"/> <nfirst>Idit</nfirst> <nlast>Shalev</nlast> <nbio>Senior lecturer in the psychology department at Ariel University, the head of the embodied cognition and self-regulation laboratory, a therapist in a private clinic, and the professional director of the Ministry of Health's training center for psychologists. <aut affid="A06" authindexid="Goergen, Maria S." listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Maria</nfirst> <nmid>Sonia</nmid> <nlast>Goergen</nlast> <nbio>Pediatric neurologist, clinical fellow of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society, supervisor and consultant P.L.A.Y. <aut affid="A07" authindexid="Vilker, Dana B." listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Dana</nfirst> <nmid>Belle</nmid> <nlast>Vilker</nlast> <nbio>Researcher in the Neuro-Cognitive Evolution lab in IIPDM, Department of Psychology, University of Haifa, and a student in the neuro-cognitive psychology master's program. Dana is also a certified service dog trainer, and the COO of True Friend - Service Dogs for Autism social project. She is combining canine-assisted therapy with service dog training for individuals with disabilities. She teaches service dog training and handling, and animal behavior and cognition, in various programs. Dana was the leader of Brainstorm HaifaU Community, which promotes the area of brain-computer interface and computational cognition both inside and outside of the academia.</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A08" authindexid="Weiss, Joshua" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Joshua</nfirst> <nlast>Weiss</nlast> <nbio>Supervising clinical psychologist currently working in private practice as well as teaching in Reichman University. My interest in understanding the psychology of criminal behavior began when I was offered an academic position in a department of criminology. I enrolled part-time to the Israeli Prison Service as a psychologist to study this population. After a number of years I was offered a senior position in the prison service, left the academic position to work in the prison, totaling 21 years and retiring early as a senior officer, at the rank of Colonel. In my private practice I continuously get referrals of adults, adolescents and children with acting out and antisocial traits. I publish clinical papers primarily focusing on countertransferential issues when assessing and treating this population. My Ph.D. is from Adelphi University, New York.</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A09" authindexid="Clark, Sarah" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Sarah</nfirst> <nlast>Clark</nlast> <nbio>Has over 16 years of experience of working within the NHS in various settings such as inpatient units, hospitals and the community with children, adolescents, and adults. Her main approach is psychoanalytic psychotherapy. She received a BSc in psychology with the Open University, and went on to study an MSc in the psychodynamics of human development with Birkbeck University of London and The British Psychotherapy Foundation. This involved a 2-year infant observation focusing on the relationship between the mother and baby, and father, as well as the baby’s physical, social and psychic development. She went on to further training with C-LAN (Centre for Leadership and Affective neuroscience). Sarah has been a webinar speaker discussing the impact of Covid and post - traumatic stress disorder on individuals, teams, and organizations’ mental health, as well as facilitating workshops for organizations, focusing on building resilience throughout this time. Sarah draws from a range of psychological approaches including mentalization based therapy, psychodynamic therapy, cognitive-behavioral therapy, and dialectical-behavioral therapy. Sarah is a member of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society and is interested in the dialogue between psychoanalysis and neuroscience.</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A10" authindexid="Biran, Iftah" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Iftah</nfirst> <nlast>Biran</nlast> <ndeg dgr="MD"/> <nbio>Psychiatrist, behavioral neurologist, and psychoanalyst. He is the chair of the Neuropsychiatric daycare ward at Tel Aviv Medical Center.</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A11" authindexid="Haim, Ilana B." listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Ilana</nfirst> <nmid>Ben</nmid> <nlast>Haim</nlast> <nbio>Born in Israel, where she lives today. She is also a graduate of the Primary Mental States advanced studies program in the psychotherapy studies in Tel Aviv University. She works as a psychotherapist mainly with children and adolescents in her private clinic, using a psychodynamic approach. Ilana is teaching psychoanalytic theory in the program for therapists in the school for psychotherapists “Yisumim Klinim” and in “Levinsky-Wingate College” in Israel and supervises students in psychotherapy programs in “Tel Aviv University” and in the “Bi National School of Psychotherapy” in Hadassah.” In addition, Ilana writes poetry. Her poetry book entitled Lo Ani “לא אני”(“Not Me”) “was published in 2016.</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A12" authindexid="Mor-Ofek, Hadas" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Hadas</nfirst> <nlast>Mor-Ofek</nlast> <nbio>Senior clinical psychologist and a supervisor. In the 18th NPSA congress, her poster “Clinical Implications of the Polyvagal Theory of the ANS in the treatment of dissociative patients’ won the “Best Poster Prize.” She has published papers concerning the clinical application of neuropsychoanalysis.</nbio></aut>

He has lectured and published extensively in the field of neuropsychoanalysis and is currently writing a PhD dissertation about complex trauma, sexuality and humor from a neuropsychoanalytic perspective at the interdisciplinary doctoral program in psychoanalysis, the psychotherapy program and the school of graduate studies, Sackler School of Medicine, Tel-Aviv University.</nbio></aut>

<aut affid="A18" authindexid="Wertman, Eli" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Eli</nfirst> <nlast>Wertman</nlast> <nbio>Behavioral neurologist who trained with Professor Ken Heilman in Gainesville, Florida. <aut affid="A19" authindexid="Elitzur, Avshalom" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Avshalom</nfirst> <nlast>Elitzur</nlast> <nbio>Physicist at the Center for Quantum Studies at Chapman University. His psychological publications span across religion, humor, and suicide prevention.</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A20" authindexid="Massardi, Elena" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Elena</nfirst> <nlast>Massardi</nlast> <ndeg dgr="MA"/> <nbio>Works in private practice as a clinical psychologist. <aut affid="A21" authindexid="Oppenheim, Lois" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Lois</nfirst> <nlast>Oppenheim</nlast> <ndeg dgr="PHD"/> <nbio>University Distinguished Scholar, Professor of French, and Chair of the Department of World Languages and Cultures at Montclair State University where she teaches courses in literature and medical humanities. She is Scholar Associate Member of the New York Psychoanalytic Society and Institute, where she is also on the faculty, and Honorary Member of the William Alanson White Institute. Dr. Oppenheim has authored or edited fifteen books, the most recent being For Want of Ambiguity: Order and Chaos in Art, Psychoanalysis, and Neuroscience (co-authored; Bloomsbury) and Imagination from Fantasy to Delusion (Routledge), awarded the Courage to Dream Prize from the American Psychoanalytic Association. <aut affid="A22" authindexid="Sharav, Dorit N." listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Dorit</nfirst> <nmid>Noy</nmid> <nlast>Sharav</nlast> <ndeg dgr="MA"/> <nbio>Senior clinical psychologist with a Master's degree in psychology from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. Dorit is a member of the Israel Psychologists Organization, the Israel Association for Psychotherapy, the Israeli Association for Couple and Family Therapy, the IRS - International Rorschach Society, and the IRI - Imago Relationship International. Dorit has presented at various national and international conferences, and has published works in Hebrew, as well as in Psychotherapy - on “Who is afraid of short-Term dynamic psychotherapy,” “On Termination and the Therapist's Personality,” 1998; in Clinical Social Work Journal - on “Good-Enough adoptive parenting and Selfobject relations,” 2002, and on “Identity concerns in Intercountry adoption,” 2006; in Rorschachiana - on The Rorschach and TAT as Relational Instrument, 2005; in Psychoanalytic Social Work, on Animating the Capacity for Concern: The Imago Couple Therapist embraces Winnicott, 2019; and in the Journal of Couple & Relationship Therapy on: Corrective Emotional Experience in Couple Therapy: An Integration between Imago approach and Psychoanalytic concepts in Light of Neuropsychological Studies, 2021.</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A23" authindexid="Danevych, Alina" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Alina</nfirst> <nlast>Danevych</nlast> <ndeg other="M.Sc."/> <nbio>Received her Master’s Degree in Biology cum laude from National University Kyiv-Mohyla Academy and a degree in psychology from T.G. Shevchenko Kyiv National University, has completed a number of training programs including EXIT training for working with refugees and people in harsh stressful situations, training in psychodrama with the Norway Moreno Institute, training in psychoanalytic theory and practice with Kyiv Institute of Modern Psychology and Psychotherapy, and training for psychodrama therapists with the Psychodrama Association for Europe (PAfE). She currently maintains or has maintained a number of support groups, is a member of and Kyiv Regional Group Coordinator for the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society (NPSA) and a member of The Ukrainian Union of Psychotherapists. <aut affid="A24" authindexid="Sherkow, Susan" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Susan</nfirst> <nlast>Sherkow</nlast> <ndeg dgr="MD"/> <nbio>Training and Supervising Analyst at the Berkshire Psychoanalytic Institute. She is co-author of Autism Spectrum Disorder: Perspectives from Psychoanalysis and Neuroscience (2014). Her most recent writings include chapter contributions: “Managing arrogance in child analysis’ in Arrogance: Developmental, Cultural, and Clinical Realms, and “Back to Freud’s beginning: Looking at Neuroscience through a Contemporary Psychoanalytic Lens’ in Psychoanalytic Trends in Theory and Practice, The Second Century of The Talking Cure. In 2012, she founded The Sherkow Center for Child Development and Autism Spectrum Disorder, a not-for-profit organization created to provide support for training, treatment, and research in the area of developmental delays and autism spectrum disorder.</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A25" authindexid="Kellman, Joshua" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Joshua</nfirst> <nlast>Kellman</nlast> <ndeg dgr="MD"/> <nbio>Child and adult psychiatrist and a psychoanalyst. <aut affid="A26" authindexid="Rosseau, Kristin" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Kristin</nfirst> <nlast>Rosseau</nlast> <ndeg dgr="MD"/> <nbio>Board-certified adult, child and adolescent psychiatrist. <aut affid="A27" authindexid="Simon, Tracey" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Tracey</nfirst> <nlast>Simon</nlast> <ndeg other="MFA"/> <ndeg dgr="LCSW"/> <ndeg other="FIPA"/> <nbio>Clinical psychoanalyst with a full-time private practice in the heart of Manhattan. <aut authindexid="Weightman, Elizabeth" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Elizabeth</nfirst> <nlast>Weightman</nlast> <nbio>Senior Lecturer at the University of Exeter and a psychoanalytic psychotherapist with experience of working in the NHS and private practice. <aut affid="A41" authindexid="Rosso, Patrizia" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Patrizia</nfirst> <nlast>Rosso</nlast> <nbio>Psychotherapist trained in Jungian analytical psychology (Turin) and neuropsychology (Padua). <aut affid="A45" authindexid="Tatti, Giovanna" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Giovanna</nfirst> <nlast>Tatti</nlast> <nbio>Milan, psychologist, psychotherapist, psychoanalyst, criminologist and criminologist lecturer. <aut affid="A48" authindexid="Peled, Ofer" listed="true" role="author"><npreti oldnpreti="Dr." type="TITLE"/> <nfirst>Ofer</nfirst> <nlast>Peled</nlast> <nbio>Senior clinical psychologist, Ruppin Academic Center - Lecturer in The MA Program in Clinical Psychology of Adulthood and Aging; Former Chair of ITA - The Israeli Association for CBT, and its representative in the EABCT - The European Association for CBT; Director of 'The Schema Therapy Center Raanana, Israel; Director of The CBT School - Individual, Family and Community Implementation in Israel. <aut affid="A49" authindexid="Laor, Ilana" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Ilana</nfirst> <nlast>Laor</nlast> <ndeg dgr="PHD"/> <nbio>Clinical psychologist and group analyst. The 22nd Annual Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society, Tel Aviv-Yafo, Israel, July 6-8, 2023: “Play: The Social Mind and Brain.”

As another year has quickly flown by, we take this opportunity to reflect on a successful annual Congress held in Tel Aviv-Yafo. The following presentation of the rich array of accepted talks that took place at our 22nd Annual Congress serves to highlight the current strength of neuropsychoanalysis and its depth and diversity when it comes to both the scientific and clinical content that it is eliciting. We are extremely grateful to our wonderful community for contributing their clinical and research work to the proceedings. We trust that the reader will enjoy the following summary of the research and symposium abstracts from the Congress and be inspired to make submissions to present at our future congresses.

Ross Balchin

Associate Editor

Email: rbalchin@npsa-association.org

Friday 7 July

Plenary symposium: Memory meets PLAY: Three perspectives from neuroscience

Mouna Maroun

Memory of fear and social interaction: Age and sex-dependent

Some memories are easy to decay, others are for a lifetime. It is well known that emotional memory and especially fear associations are acquired in one trial learning and are hard to extinguish. Most of our knowledge on the mechanisms mediating fear and extinction were obtained from adult male rodents. Much less is known whether these mechanisms are the same in the juvenile animal or in females. We have a plethora of data addressing differences between adult and juvenile rats in their mechanisms of extinction while mainly focusing on the neuromodulator oxytocin. Oxytocin is critical for social behavior; our studies shed light on the interaction between social behavior and extinction of fear while addressing possible differences between adults and juveniles, males and females. These findings can be relevant when considering how to treat boys and girls suffering from stress-related disorders.

45th Bulletin of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society

Bulletin 45 offers thirteen group reports from all around the world - Romania, Siberia, the United Kingdom, Japan, the Netherlands, Spain, Mexico, Israel, Lithuania, Sweden, Turkey, and the United States. We think you will agree that the Neuropsychoanalysis Association has a vibrant and well-functioning SEEKING system. Some groups have been active since 2011 and have shown an increasing enthusiasm as seen in our latest Bulletins. Our curious and creative members join together to read, design and execute experiments, write papers and books, and translate books into their native languages. Several groups report their interest in affective neuroscience, defense mechanisms, and psychopathology. These reports speak to the ongoing commitment among our members to the interdisciplinary learning and dialogue that bring us together, continuously expanding and developing neuropsychoanalytic theory and practice. The contributions of our regional groups leave no doubt that, as we enter year 26 of the journal, we stand on a solid foundation with formidable energy to move our work forward. This bulletin highlights the development of ideas, projects, and research that keeps neuropsychoanalysis active all around the world.

Ana Delgadillo Hernández

a.delgadillo@npsa-association.org

Jane Abrams

jabramsdsw@gmail.com

The Bucharest Neuropsychoanalysis Group

The Bucharest Neuropsychoanalysis Group, Romania, was established in the spring of 2022 but intensified its activities starting in 2023, when the group began to grow, already counting 16 members. The group includes seven psychoanalytic psychotherapists, two integrative psychotherapists, one therapist specializing in EMDR and trauma work, as well as four clinical psychologists and two students. The group meets once a month, on the first or last Saturday of the month, for three hours. In addition to these in-person meetings, the group has come together several times throughout the year in various contexts and workshops, which will be mentioned below.

Hessel Boerboom  

Maurice Nadelman (1990) noted that Freud's article “Psychical Treatment” (1894) could be seen as the basis for modern psychosomatic treatment.1 In that paper, Freud indeed lays a basis for a psychosomatic treatment of some physiological ills. However, the relation soma-mind or mind-soma seemed to divide the therapists and the research in later years: in some quarters, a focus on the somatic explanation even for psychic ailments; in others, a disregard of the somatic components of psychic disturbances.

One of the notable exceptions to this divide has been the Paris Psychosomatic School, which has sought to keep the complementary view alive. This began with Pierre Marty, who, together with Michel de M’Uzan, developed the idea of “mechanical thinking” whereby normal psychological defences and structures break down and so lead to somatization. Stora, Marilia Aisenstein, and Claude Smadja introduced the “second generation” where the ideas of Green and Winnicott are leading to a further development of the ideas of the “first generation.” Since 2000, Stora, an exponent of this second generation, has been the founder/leader of the French Group of Psychoanalysis, Medicine and Neuroscience, a regional group of the NPSA, and has sought to integrate neuropsychoanalysis in what he calls “neuropsychosomatics” (Dodds, 2008). France is by no means the only country where psychosomatics plays a role in health services although it is often not so closely related to psychoanalysis as in the Paris School. For example, in the USA or Germany, we see consultation-liaison psychiatry, which seems to resemble the role of psychosomatics that Stora describes (Diefenbacher, 2004; Levenson, 2019).

Stora is a psychosomatist. He interviews the patients, referred to him by the medical staff, to get a picture of the whole patient: his life, his history. He thus explores the relationship between psychic functioning and somatic disorders, not because the mind is the cause of the somatic disorder, but because the mind participates in all diseases. His integrative psychosomatic is based on the principle that the central nervous system is fundamental in the mind-body relation. Stora argues that we are confronted with excitations of varying degrees. Alongside the immune system, our psychic system forms a line of defense. When these defenses are overwhelmed, we see pathology. Treating the body without healing the mind, may cause the movement of disorders from one disease to another. The Psychosomatic Therapy Casebook is the third book by Stora on the subject that is translated into English. The two earlier books (Stora, 2007, 2015) had a commending foreword by Mark Solms, and I agree with the recommendation; reading those books does add to one's understanding of this third book.

Introduction

This book is the first in the Routledge Neuropsychoanalysis series edited by Mark Solms. Mark Kinet is a well-known writer in the Dutch-speaking psychoanalytical community, who has published over 30 books. This book is an updated and expanded translation of an earlier Dutch book.

Kinet tells us how, out of his curious nature, he encountered neuropsychoanalysis. First through his professional connection with Ariane Bazan, then reading and viewing YouTube videos of Mark Solms. As he tells us, he is neither an academic nor a neuropsychoanalyst, but he has been working for more than thirty years as a psychiatrist and a psychoanalyst. The book includes 21 chapters that are separated by short interludes associatively connected to the chapters. Two-thirds of the book are about his discovery of neuropsychoanalysis, as explained by Solms. The last third of the book links Solms’ neuropsychoanalysis to the ideas of Bazan and, hence, to the ideas of Lacan.

Summary

Kinet describes his discovery of neuropsychoanalysis with a short personal introduction and in the following interlude we are introduced to Panksepp’s seven emotional-instinctive systems that we share with all mammals through Bruce, the black Labrador that lives in Kinet’s family. So, the groundwork is laid: our emotions are linked to our brain structures.

As Kinet is a trained psychiatrist, he was at first, as he tells us in the next chapter, skeptical of the contribution of neurology to his understanding of his patients, each a unique human being.

In the following chapters, we learn about neuroplasticity and the neurobiology of attachment, which is so important for our first memories. This leads to Freud’s Project and Solms’ “translation” in neuropsychoanalytical terms, which describes that our memory helps to satisfy our needs. And so, we meet Panksepp and his affect taxonomy and the meaning of homeostasis. The scene is set for Solms’ ground-breaking insight that the id is conscious. And then the most recent “addition” to the neuropsychoanalytical model which is the free-energy principle and active inference as proposed by Friston. The last chapter in the first two-thirds concerns the clinical implications.

In his article “Unsuccessful Accommodations: Reconceptualizing the Psychopathology Attributed to Neuropsychological Deficits,” Joseph Palombo (2023) challenges the linear view that a diagnosis of a condition with neuropsychological deficits will result in a predetermined outcome. He defines such disorders or syndromes with neurocognitive deficits - for example, dyslexia, executive functioning disorders, and nonverbal learning disabilities - as limitations of the person’s capacity to perform a task that is required of them. Considered neuroatypical, people with neuropsychological deficits often cannot succeed in what they wish to accomplish. The deficits often are multidimensional and can include cooccurrences in more than one area. He uses the term “unsuccessful accommodations” to describe the neuroatypical person’s failures to achieve their goals.

Palombo’s central argument is that a neuropsychological deficit does not necessarily predict an unsuccessful accommodation. His focus is on the complexity of each individual and their interactions with their environments. Outcomes depend on multiple factors, such as the nature of the disorder, the strengths of the individual, temperament, and conditions in the person’s environment. “Successful accommodation may result when deficits are complemented by others who provide the missing function or when the environment can be modified” (p. 8).

Palombo emphasizes the role of a person’s subjectivity and the ways in which their deficits filter their experience, affecting the meanings they construct of their experiences. Unsuccessful accommodations can lead to feelings of shame, attempts to hide deficits, defenses such as disavowal and dissociation - all of which can interfere with relationships. Palombo refers to these experiences of shame, fear of exposure, and humiliation as forming “nuclei of narcissistic injuries” which become “attractors or nodal points around which patterns of thoughts, feelings or behaviors are organized” (p. 11). If a person is unaware of the cause of a deficit, they will construct a narrative in order to integrate their experiences, and this narrative will inform their expectations concerning how others will respond to them. Their narratives are often not an accurate assessment of how others see them, and this can lead to unsuccessful accommodations. According to Palombo, attractors are the result of sets of experiences that have particular emotional salience to the person and form “… enduring patterns of responses or interactions that become encoded either in declarative or non-declarative memory” (p. 12). The patterns manifest in behavior, feelings, thoughts, and fantasies.

Pain, somatoform pain, questionnaire, development, validation

Somatoform pain poses major challenges in medicine. There is a lack of quantitative instruments that systematically assess psychosocial aspects of somatoform pain. A better knowledge of such aspects could contribute (1) to gaining further insight into the relationship between psychodynamic and psychosocial components of pain, and (2) to facilitating the development and monitoring of improved interventions targeting psychodynamic and psychosocial mechanisms of pain. An item pool on biopsychosocial aspects of pain was developed and completed by 200 patients with somatoform pain disorder. In addition, anxiety (STAI), depression (BDI II), somatization (SOMS-2), and quality of life (SF-36) were assessed. As compared to norm data, patients reported higher scores for anxiety (STAI), depression (BDI-II) somatization (SMOS-2), and lower quality of life (SF-36). Applying item and factor analyses, a new questionnaire (QSP-31) was developed to identify psychodynamic and psychosocial aspects of pain. There was evidence for the construct validity of the six scales through confirmatory factor analysis: Relationships between pain and negative emotions, Negative attitudes towards help-seeking, Negative pain-related childhood experiences, Negative attitudes towards own body, Negative aspects of the doctor-patient relationship, and Perceived pain control. Cronbach's alpha coefficients for these scales lay within the range of .81-.92. Regarding criterion validity, moderate correlations in expected directions were found between all scales and anxiety, depression, somatic symptom severity, and quality of life, except for the scale Perceived pain control. The QSP-31 appears promising for the identification of relevant psychosocial aspects associated with the experience of pain and might be a useful instrument.

Repression, unconscious, psychoanalysis, mechanistic model

In recent philosophical and (neuro)psychological discussions of phenomena such as motivated forgetting, memory inhibition, self-deception, and implicit bias, various authors have suggested that repression might be a useful notion to make sense of these phenomena, or that these phenomena indeed provide evidence for repression. However, surprisingly, these claims usually do not rely on any explicit model of repression. Consequently, it remains unclear whether invoking repression in these discussions is justified. In this paper, I propose a psychological “how-possibly” model that can serve as a basis for scientific research that I call the hybrid model of repression. This model combines the advantages while avoiding the problems of two types of models of repression – the higher-order model and the separation model – that have been discussed and defended by different authors and that both have their origin in Freud. This “how-possibly” model may then set the stage for further empirical research, which can form the basis for a “how-actually” model in the longer run.

Pathological lying, pseudologia fantastica, amnesia, schizo-paranoid position, depressive position, manic defense

Following bilateral hippocampal damage caused by an acute stroke superimposed on an old, previously undiagnosed stroke, Mr. S, a 54-year-old man with narcissistic-psychopathic traits and a long-standing history of pathological lying, was admitted to our ward. He presented with anterograde amnesia and claimed he had lost his ability to lie. Mr. S underwent extensive neuropsychological testing and psychodynamically oriented psychotherapy one to two times per week. His emotional responses fluctuated between perceiving the stroke as both his salvation and his punishment, viewing the therapist as either caring or punitive, and regarding himself as omnipotent yet helpless. The medical team was similarly divided, with some viewing the patient as a malingerer and others perceiving him as severely impaired. We interpreted these polarized responses both from the patient and the medical team as consistent with a paranoid-schizoid position. From a neurofunctional perspective, we propose that these fluctuations were linked to the patient's fragmented perception across multiple domains, including memory, time, space, body, and self, alongside an impairment in his body's structural representation. Dynamically, we suggest that the patient's inability to lie revealed his underlying difficulty in tolerating the depressive position without the protective shield provided by his habitual pathological lying. We conclude that hippocampal function plays a crucial role in the psychopathology of pathological lying. Specifically, we propose that the creation of pathological lies relies on the same anatomical structures involved in memory formation. Dynamically, we argue that pathological lies serve a similar function to the manic defense, protecting against an unbearable depressive position.

<aut affid="A01" authindexid="Balchin, Ross" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Ross</nfirst> <nlast>Balchin</nlast> <nti>Associate Editor</nti></aut>
<aut affid="A02" authindexid="Davis, Kenneth L." listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Kenneth</nfirst> <nmid>L.</nmid> <nlast>Davis</nlast> <nbio>Co-author with Jaak Panksepp of the Affective Neuroscience Personality Scales and co-author with Jaak Panksepp of The Emotional Foundations of Personality (2018). Ken is also the co-author with Christian Montag of Animal Emotions. Ken's primary interests are the assessment of personality and the application of neuroscience research to further a broad understanding of personality ranging from troubled to fulfilled human lives</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A03" authindexid="Markova, Elena" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Elena</nfirst> <nlast>Markova</nlast> <nbio>Ph.D. in molecular genetics, psychoanalytic psychotherapist, clinical psychologist, Moscow Institute of Psychoanalysis, Moscow, Russia</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A04" authindexid="Baser, Ibrahim G." listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Ibrahim</nfirst> <nmid>Goksin</nmid> <nlast>Baser</nlast> <nbio>Clinical psychologist based in Istanbul, Turkey, holds a doctoral degree in clinical psychology from both Fatih Sultan Mehmet Vakif University and Istanbul Medeniyet University. His doctoral research focuses on exploring the interplay between emotional regulation difficulties, defensive styles, and dark triad personality traits. During his master's studies, he received comprehensive training in systemically oriented family and couple therapy, narrative therapy, and cognitive behavioral therapy. His academic pursuits took a turn towards affective neuroscience and neuropsychoanalysis after encountering the work of Jaak Panksepp. Currently serving as a research assistant at Fatih Sultan Mehmet Vakif University, Ibrahim Goksin Baser also maintains a private practice as a psychotherapist. His professional journey reflects a commitment to both academic research and practical application within the field of clinical psychology</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A05" authindexid="Bulfon, Matteo" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Matteo</nfirst> <nlast>Bulfon</nlast> <nbio>M.A. in Psychology at University of Trieste (UniTs), Italy – Specialization in Psychotherapy (psychoanalytically oriented) at the “Scuola Di Psicoterapia Psicoanalitica” of Ravenna, Trieste office – Working in private practice and in public service (for addictions) – Currently research fellow (Borsa di Studio) at the Institute for Maternal and Child Health – IRCCS “Burlo Garofolo,” Trieste, Italy, in two research projects: “Meaning of symptom and psychological support in patients with functional disorders” and “Informative and educational interventions in patients with endometriosis” – Completed the clinical training course, based on neuropsychoanalytic knowledge, linked to the NPSA society, hosted by Dr Andrea Clarici in Trieste, Italy (2023; registered and participating in the 2024 group) – Presented an accepted poster at the NPSA 2023 Congress on the subject of FND</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A06" authindexid="Caruso, Paola" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Paola</nfirst> <nlast>Caruso</nlast> <nbio>Works as a Neurologist at the Neurological Clinic of Trieste, in the Stroke Unit. She is an expert in stroke recognition and treatment. She is also a sonographer taking care of doppler ultrasounds of epiaortic vessels and intracranial vessels. Over the past number of years, she has been working with the psychotherapists and psychiatrists taking care of patients with functional neurological disorders. We treat FND patients both in the emergency setting and in outpatient management</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A07" authindexid="Vales, Lisandro" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Lisandro</nfirst> <nlast>Vales</nlast> <nbio>(Member of the International Neuropsychoanalsis Society) has a PhD in Psychology with orientation in Cognitive Neuroscience, and MSc in Psychoneuroinmunoendocrinology, and a bachelor's degree in Psychology. Postgraduate in psychoanalytic psychotherapy, Postgraduate in couple, families, and group psychoanalysis. He is an associate professor at the Faculty of Psychology, University of Republic. He has been teaching: Psychoanalysis (1998–2008) Neurobiology and Neuropsychology (2009–2017), Psychological Theories (2018–today), Member of the Traumatic Brain Injury rehabilitation team, Department of Neuropsychology of the Hospital de Clínicas, University of Republic (2010–2017), Member of the Preventive Assistance Psychological Care Service (SAPPA) Faculty of Psychology in the University of Republic (2012–today). Professor, Director, and currently Rector of the Francisco de Asís University Institute (2010–today). He is a neuropsychology and clinical psychologist who has also worked with adults, families, groups, and health teams in hospitals. He has conducted research on TBI patients, psychodynamic psychotherapy, and in social sports projects</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A08" authindexid="Limony, Eyal" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Eyal</nfirst> <nlast>Limony</nlast> <nbio>Psychiatrist. He specializes in somatic symptom disorders as well as in the neuropsychiatry of Parkinson's Disease. He works in the Division of Psychiatry at Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A09" authindexid="Barzel-Raveh, Irith" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Irith</nfirst> <nlast>Barzel-Raveh</nlast> <nbio>Senior clinical psychologist, the chairperson of the Israeli Neuropsychoanalysis Society, and a member of the Executive Committee of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society. She was the former co-chair of the scientific committee of the Israeli Association of Psychotherapy. Irith was also head clinical psychologist of the Neuro Pediatric Unit in the Tel Aviv area, the Infant Development clinic, and of 26 well babies clinics. She was coordinator of the “Normalcy in Infancy” seminar at Tel Aviv University Medical School, and of the International Seminar of “Ferenczi in the clinic” with seven groups working around the Globe. She is the owner of Neuropsychoanalysis – Open school website, which enhances neuropsychoanalysis congresses and theoretical seminars for the Neuropsychoanalysis Society. She also works at her private clinic. She completed her PhD under the supervision of Professor Aner Govrin and Professor Mark Solms. She is on the board of the Goldman Fund for Clinical Psychologists</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A10" authindexid="Weiss, Joshua" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Joshua</nfirst> <nlast>Weiss</nlast> <nbio>Supervising clinical psychologist and has been studying neuropsychoanalysis with Prof. Solms in case conferences for the past five years. He worked in psychiatric hospitals for five years and then in the Israel Prison Service for 21 years, retiring eight years ago at the rank of Colonel. He completed his doctoral training in Adelphi University, New York, and has been teaching for 30 years, currently at Reichman University. His private practice includes treating severely disturbed people and forensic cases</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A11" authindexid="Weisman, Ynon" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Ynon</nfirst> <nlast>Weisman</nlast> <nbio>Clinical psychologist from Tel Aviv. He has been working with survivors of trauma and loss in different clinical settings for the past decade. A student of Prof. Solms in his clinical seminars for the last six years, he now teaches a neuropsychoanalytic perspective for clinical practice. Ynon is also a certified Intensive-Short Term Dynamic Psychotherapist and incorporates both perspectives in his clinical work, teaching, and research. Since October 7th he has been working with survivors of the Re’im Music Festival Massacre</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A12" authindexid="Mizen, Susan" listed="true" role="author"><npreti oldnpreti="Dr" type="TITLE"/> <nfirst>Susan</nfirst> <nlast>Mizen</nlast> <nbio>Jungian Analyst and worked as a Consultant Psychiatrist in Psychotherapy in the NHS in Exeter for 25 years. She developed a psychotherapeutic day and outpatient program in Exeter as an alternative to locked placements for patients with severe personality disorder. Her relational affective model is an analytic, neuro-scientific approach to therapeutic work with this patient group. She investigated the model in a neuroscience PhD at The University of Exeter. She also works in private practice in Exeter as an Analytical Psychologist. She is a Fellow of the Royal College of Psychiatrists where she chaired the Psychotherapy Faculty Executive between 2014 and 2018. She is currently chair of the Talking Therapies Task Force making the health economic case for a national program of psychotherapy for hospitalized patients with severe personality disorder</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A13" authindexid="Britton, Ron" listed="true" role="author"><npreti oldnpreti="Dr" type="TITLE"/> <nfirst>Ron</nfirst> <nlast>Britton</nlast> <ndeg other="FRCPsych."/> <nbio>Distinguished Fellow British Psychoanal. Soc. Educated at Lancaster Royal Grammar School and UCL, London, medically qualified 1973: postgraduate training, neurology Queen’s Square, adult and child psychiatry Mausdsley London, child psychotherapy and adult psychoanalytic training, Tavistock Clinic and British Psychoanalytical Society. IPA Award for Outstanding Scientific Achievement in 2013, and The Sigourney Award (USA) for Outstanding Psychoanalytic Contributions, in 2014. Author of Belief & Imagination (1998), Sex, Death and the Super Ego (2003 2nd, Ed. 2018), and Between Mind and Brain (2015). Retired from psychoanalytic clinical practice in 2022 but remains active in psychoanalytic teaching and research</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A14" authindexid="Clarici, Andrea" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Andrea</nfirst> <nlast>Clarici</nlast> <ndeg dgr="MD"/> <nbio>Psychoanalytic psychotherapist and psychiatrist from Trieste, Italy, working clinically in private psychoanalytic practice. He is also a professor in the course “Advanced Dynamic Psychology” at the Faculty of Psychology and the course “Child Neuropsychiatry” at the Faculty of Medicine, both at the University of Trieste (UNITS, Italy). He trained at the Centro Studi di Psicoterapia Psicoanalitica e Metodologia Istituzionale in Milan with psychoanalysts supervised and inspired by Joseph Sandler (IPA President 1989–1993) and his wife, Ann-Marie. Andrea Clarici is the chief coordinator of the Centro di Formazione e Ricerca in Psicoterapia Psicoanalitica (CFR; director Dr. Andrea Zanettovich) in Trieste. He has worked psychoanalytically with brain-lesioned patients and is currently involved in a project on individual psychoanalytic psychotherapy for patients with neurofunctional (conversion) disorders at the Neurological Clinic of the University of Trieste. He is also on the executive committee of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society as International Liaison Officer. He translated into Italian The Archeology of Mind by Jaak Panksepp and Lucy Biven, Clinical Studies in Neuro-psychoanalysis by Karen Kaplan-Solms and Mark Solms, and The Brain and the Inner World by Mark Solms and Oliver Turnbull. In 2018, he edited a collection of selected works of Mark Solms, ranging from 1997 to 2017, in a book with the title La coscienza dell’Es [The Conscious Id], all these books for Raffaello Cortina Publisher (Milan). In 2024, he also translated Solms’ The Hidden Spring [La fonte nascosta, in Italian] for Adelphi Editore (Milan)</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A15" authindexid="Dall'Aglio, John" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>John</nfirst> <nlast>Dall'Aglio</nlast> <nbio>Graduate student in clinical psychology at Duquesne University. His clinical and scholarly research focuses on Lacanian neuropsychoanalysis. He also teaches neuropsychoanalysis in undergraduate courses. He has published several articles on neuropsychoanalysis and is the author of the forthcoming book (tentatively titled) A Lacanian Neuropsychoanalysis: Affective Consciousness, Predictive Coding, Sex, and Jouissance (Palgrave). He is the winner of the 2021 New Author Prize from the Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A16" authindexid="Biran, Iftah" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Iftah</nfirst> <nlast>Biran</nlast> <nbio>Psychoanalyst, behavioral neurologist and psychiatrist. He chairs the Neuropsychiatric Daycare Ward at the Division of Psychiatry in Tel Aviv Sourasky Medical Center. He specialized in treating patients with conversion disorder. He is Co-Editor of Neuropsychoanalysis</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A17" authindexid="Tomatis, Davide" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Davide</nfirst> <nlast>Tomatis</nlast> <nbio>Psychologist and psychoanalytical psychotherapist, is a private psychotherapist in Turin, Italy, and a member of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society and the Istituto Mitchell in Turin. He’s interested in the relationship between neuroscience and psychoanalysis, in particular in psychotherapy for brain-injured people</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A18" authindexid="Boonstra, Evert" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Evert</nfirst> <nlast>Boonstra</nlast> <nbio>Postdoc with Mark Solms at the University of Cape Town. Prior to this appointment, Boonstra completed a Ph.D. in cognitive neuroscience at the Vrije Universiteit in Amsterdam, and Boonstra completed a Master's program in both cognitive neuroscience and philosophy. Boonstra is interested in the intersections between neuroscience, philosophy, and psychoanalysis</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A19" authindexid="Brienza, Lorenzo" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Lorenzo</nfirst> <nlast>Brienza</nlast> <nbio>Currently a Ph.D. candidate at the Department of Psychology, University of Turin, Italy. Lorenzo is strongly fascinated by the Pankseppian Affective Neuroscience field, particularly in its application in the clinical, personological, and etiological domains. His research mainly focuses on psychological assessment, the affective neuroscience approach to personality, evolutionary psychopathology, and dimensional and transdiagnostic models of psychopathology</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A20" authindexid="Barry, Virginia" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Virginia</nfirst> <nlast>Barry</nlast> <nbio>Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst in full-time private practice in Chicago. She has been on the Faculty of the Chicago Psychoanalytic Institute since 1991. She has taught many clinical and theoretical courses to psychiatric residents and psychoanalytic candidates. For more than two decades she has taught a course entitled “Mind & Brain” that introduces candidates to areas of neuroscience and cognitive science that have relevance for clinical and theoretical psychoanalysis. She is especially interested in thinking about the biology of meaning, the development of language from gesture, the isomorphism between the hierarchical organization of the brain and that of the mind, and the alterations of agency and motivation during the course of a psychoanalysis. Her book Scratch and Sniff Proust reflects all her interests integrating psychoanalysis, literature, neuroscience and cognitive science, art and the sense of smell (<url>scratchandsniffproust.com</url>). Dr Barry is an associate editor of Neuropsychoanalysis</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A21" authindexid="Turnbull, Oliver" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Oliver</nfirst> <nlast>Turnbull</nlast> <nbio>Neuropsychologist (and a clinical psychologist), with an interest in emotion and its many consequences for mental life. His interests include: emotion-based learning, and the experience that we describe as “intuition”; the role of emotion in false beliefs, especially in neurological patients; emotion regulation, and the neuroscience of psychotherapy. He is the author of some 200 scientific articles on these topics. He is also the author (together with Mark Solms) of the popular science text The Brain and the Inner World, and (with Christian Salas and Rudi Coetzer) of a textbook for clinical trainees: Mistakes in Clinical Neuropsychology: Learning from a Case-based Approach. He is a Professor of Neuropsychology in Bangor University, Wales, where he is also Deputy Vice Chancellor. In Bangor he runs an annual neuroanatomy course, the Visceral Mind Summer School, based on learning through drawing and painting brains</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A22" authindexid="Tatti, Giovanna" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Giovanna</nfirst> <nlast>Tatti</nlast> <nbio>Psychologist, psychotherapist, psychoanalyst A.S.P. – Association of Psychoanalytic Studies and IFPS – International Federation of Psychoanalytic Societies; full member of PDLab and ISTFP – International Society for Transference Focused Psychotherapy; member of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society; TFP graduate, EMDR practitioner. She is also a prison psychologist with training in forensic psychopathology, clinical criminology and youth justice mediation. Member of AISTED – Italian Association for the Study of Trauma and Dissociation and ESTD – European Society of Trauma and Dissociation. Member of SIC – Italian Society of Criminology and Mito&Realtà – Association for Therapeutic Communities and Residences. Clinical experience in both private and institutional settings. Lecturer in various masters and postgraduate courses; author of articles and books. Special interests in trauma, dissociative functions and the specificity of transference and countertransference relationships and violence</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A23" authindexid="Henningsen, Peter" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Peter</nfirst> <nlast>Henningsen</nlast> <ndeg dgr="MD"/> <nbio>Professor and head, Dept. of Psychosomatic Medicine and Psychotherapy, Technical University of Munich, Germany. Spokesperson of German university professors of Psychosomatic Medicine. Member of the Medical Committee of the German Science and Humanities Council (WR). Board certification in neurology and in psychosomatic medicine and psychotherapy. Special interest in persistent and functional somatic symptoms, e.g. coordinator of German national guidelines on the topic</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A24" authindexid="Van Den Houte, Maaike" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Maaike</nfirst> <nlast>Van Den Houte</nlast> <ndeg dgr="PHD"/> <nbio>Postdoctoral researcher at the Laboratory of Brain-Gut Axis Studies at the University of Leuven in Belgium. As an experimental health psychologist, Maaike received her PhD in 2017, in which she investigated symptom perception processes in patients with fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue. Her current focus is to study the broad biopsychosocial mechanisms underlying functional somatic syndromes through mechanistic translation patient studies using experimental design as well as neuroimaging including PET and fMRI. The numerous mechanisms she studies in these patient groups – with a focus on chronic fatigue and irritable bowel syndrome – include interoception and symptom perception, function of the stress response systems, gut-brain interactions, as well as peripheral – and neuro-inflammation</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A25" authindexid="Lane, Richard" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Richard</nfirst> <nlast>Lane</nlast> <ndeg dgr="MD"/> <ndeg dgr="PHD"/> <nbio>Professor of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience at the University of Arizona. A clinical psychiatrist, psychodynamic psychotherapist and neuroscientist, he is the author of over 200 papers and book chapters and senior editor of two books. The central theme of his scholarly and clinical work has been emotion and its contribution to physical and mental health. He has actively pursued research on the behavioral, neuroanatomical and clinical correlates of emotional awareness and has performed numerous neuroimaging studies of emotion and emotional awareness using PET and fMRI. A special interest has been the role of impaired emotional awareness in functional somatic syndromes. His model of enduring change in psychotherapy due to memory reconsolidation in interaction with emotion was the basis for a teaching and research fellowship in 2023 sponsored by Fulbright Austria and the Sigmund Freud Museum in Vienna. Other honors include being a Distinguished Life Fellow of the American Psychiatric Association, elected member of the American College of Neuropsychopharmacology, Honorary Fellow of the American College of Psychoanalysts, President of the American Psychosomatic Society (in 2006) and recipient of their Distinguished Scientist Award (in 2024)</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A26" authindexid="Subic-Wrana, Claudia" listed="true" role="author"><npreti oldnpreti="Priv. Doz. Dr. rer. medic." type="TITLE"/> <nfirst>Claudia</nfirst> <nlast>Subic-Wrana</nlast> <nbio>Psychoanalyst (DPV/ IPA) has worked for more than two decades in the psychosomatic departments of the university hospitals in Cologne and Mainz, Germany. This fostered her interest in emotion regulation and psychotherapy research, which became her main fields of research. She is a longtime collaborator of Richard Lane, and translated the LEAS into German. Together they published several empirical studies on the Levels of Emotional Awareness in patients suffering from psychosomatic disorders and theoretical papers on working with emotions in different psychotherapeutic modalities. Today she works in private practice, and is chair of the Psychoanalytische Arbeitsgemeinschaft Köln-Düsseldorf, a DPV/ IPA training institute</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A27" authindexid="Uccellini, Orlando" listed="true" role="author"><npreti oldnpreti="Dr" type="TITLE"/> <nfirst>Orlando</nfirst> <nlast>Uccellini</nlast> <nbio>Child and adolescent neuropsychiatrist and psychoanalyst with extensive experience in public work. He started his career as a neuropsychiatrist and psychoanalyst working with children and adolescents with acute mental disorders at the NPI of San Gerardo Hospital in Monza, then in an outpatient clinic. His professional career has been characterized by eclecticism, with a focus on EMDR therapy. In recent years he has been passionate about interventions in early life and perinatal clinical psychology, and for over a decade has been a supervisor and trainer at the National Association for the Defense of the Abandoned Child in Milan. He is on the Board of Directors of the University Master's Program “WeCare Professionals: Prevention and Intervention in the First 1000 Days of Life” at the Universities of Brescia and Milano Bicocca. He is the founder of the experimental outpatient clinic “1000days: wecaregeneration,” which focuses on the early treatment of traumatized mothers and children up to the age of three</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A28" authindexid="Uccella, Sara" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Sara</nfirst> <nlast>Uccella</nlast> <nbio>Child neuropsychiatrist and psychotherapist with special training in early childhood development and sleep physiology. She is working on a research project on prematurity and mental development. She collaborates with the Department of Neonatology and Child Neuropsychiatry at the Giannina Gaslini Hospital in Genoa and the Hopital CHU Lenval in Nice to develop care pathways for families of neurologically vulnerable infants and children and adolescents with neurological (including rare) and psychiatric conditions. She has studied and worked in several European and non-European cities exploring the relationship between mind and body. She has published in international scientific journals</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A29" authindexid="Montirosso, Rosario" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Rosario</nfirst> <nlast>Montirosso</nlast> <nbio>Psychologist and Psychotherapist. He is the Director of the 0–3 Center for Children with Developmental Disabilities at the IRCCS “E. Medea” – “La Nostra Famiglia” Association in Bosisio Parini (LC). He carries out his clinical work in the field of parenting and social-emotional development in the first years of life of children at risk. Since 2006 he has introduced in Italy the use of the NNNS Infant Neurobehavioral Rating Scale and the collaborative consultation approach to support parenting at risk. He is a member of the steering committee of the Care Group of the Italian Society of Neonatology and of the European Foundation for the Care of Newborn Infants (EFCNI) Topic Expert Group on patient- and family-centered developmental supportive care. He has conducted studies on the quality of the early mother–child relationship in both normal and atypical conditions (e.g. prematurity), and has been investigating epigenetic changes caused by exposure to early life stressors, and the effects of interpersonal touch in early childhood development. He collaborates with several national and international early childhood research centers, and has been Principal Investigator or Principal Collaborator on more than 15 research projects funded by the Ministry of Health. He is the author of more than 100 peer-reviewed articles published in international journals. He has edited several book chapters in Italian and English</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A30" authindexid="Rosanova, Mario" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Mario</nfirst> <nlast>Rosanova</nlast> <nbio>Graduated in Medicine and Surgery in 2001. He is Associate Professor of Human Physiology at the University of Milan, where he works in the research group of Prof. Marcello Massimini. He has dedicated the last 15 years of his research to the development of a technique combining transcranial magnetic stimulation and electroencephalogram (TMS-EEG) for the study of human cortical circuits in physiological states, such as wakefulness and sleep, and in pathological states, such as disorders of consciousness following severe brain injury. He has co-authored more than 50 scientific publications in international peer-reviewed journals (<url>https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=6li4Ay0AAAAJ&hl=en</url>) and eight book chapters</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A31" authindexid="Brooks, Samantha" listed="true" role="author"><npreti oldnpreti="Dr" type="TITLE"/> <nfirst>Samantha</nfirst> <nlast>Brooks</nlast> <nbio>Chartered member of the British Psychological Society, and is currently a Reader in Cognitive Neuroscience at the School of Psychology, Faculty of Health, Liverpool John Moores University, UK. Previously, Dr. Brooks worked as a lecturer for six years in the Department of Psychiatry, University of Cape Town, South Africa. Dr Brooks’ research specializes in the neural mechanisms of impulse and appetite control in various psychiatric conditions (e.g. addiction, eating disorders). Previously, she completed her postdoctoral fellowship at Uppsala University, Sweden, where she continues to collaborate on projects examining the brain processes underlying eating disorders. She gained her Ph.D. at the Institute of Psychiatry, King's College, London, where she learned clinical neuroimaging techniques, such as structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging. Dr Brooks has published over 100 papers, including 6 book chapters, to date in high impact journals/books, and continues to present at international conferences. Her work on impulse control in eating disorders and addiction has so far attracted over 1 million Euros in international funding, and collaborations with experts in the United Kingdom, Sweden, Italy, South Africa and the United States</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A32" authindexid="Van Geenhoven, Veerle" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Veerle</nfirst> <nlast>Van Geenhoven</nlast> <nbio>Small animal veterinarian who received her B.vet.sc. degree from Antwerp University (B) and M.vet.med. degree from Ghent University (B). Her veterinary career was preceded by an academic career as a linguist/formal semanticist (Ph.D., Eberhard-Karls-Universität Tübingen (D), PD Dr. habil., Goethe-Universität, Frankfurt (D)). Her major research interests are the human-animal bond from a neuropsychoanalytic perspective, species-independent theory of mind, psychogenic somatic disease in domesticated animals, and the role of animals in mental health research. She is also engaged in implementing Balint work for veterinarians</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A33" authindexid="Leuzinger-Bohleber, Marianne" listed="true" role="author"><npreti oldnpreti="Prof. Dr. Phil" type="TITLE"/> <nfirst>Marianne</nfirst> <nlast>Leuzinger-Bohleber</nlast> <nbio>Director of the Sigmund-Freud-Institut in Frankfurt a.M., Germany (2001–2016), professor em. for psychoanalysis at the University of Kassel, Senior Research Fellow at the Universitymedicine in Mainz. She is training analyst of the German Psychoanalytical Association (DPV) and the International Psychoanalytical Association (IPA). Chair of the Research Subcommittees for Clinical, Conceptual, Epistemological and Historical Research of the IPA (2001–2009), Vice Chair for Europe of the Research Board of the IPA 2010–2021; Chair of the IPA Subcommittee for Migration and Refugees 2018/19. Since then member of the committee. She received the Mary Sigourney Award 2016, the Haskell Norman Prize for Excellence in Psychoanalysis 2017, the Robert S. Wallerstein Fellowship (2022–2027), and the IPA’s Outstanding Scientific Achievement Award, 2023. Her research fields are clinical and extraclinical research in psychoanalysis, psychoanalytical developmental research, prevention studies, interdisciplinary dialogue between psychoanalysis and literature, educational sciences and the neurosciences</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A34" authindexid="Sengul, Pinar" listed="true" role="author"><npreti oldnpreti="Dr" type="TITLE"/> <nfirst>Pinar</nfirst> <nlast>Sengul</nlast> <nbio>Turkish neuroscientist with a diverse international background, holds a PhD in Neuroscience from Acibadem University. Specializing in neurodegeneration, she excels in biochemical techniques, clinical data collection, and advanced statistical analysis. Driven by a passion for understanding the interplay of diet, sleep, memory, and neurodegenerative diseases, her groundbreaking research at the University of London has earned international acclaim. Proficient in neuroimaging techniques (fMRI, EEG, fNIRS) and neurochemical methods (NMR), she also holds an MSc in Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuropsychology from the University of London. With a strong presence in clinical neuropsychology across Germany, England, and Norway, Dr Sengul is committed to unraveling the complexities of the brain. Her impactful research has been featured in global newspapers like The Independent and The Daily Mail, and she has been a sought-after expert on TV programs from the UK to Norway. Fluent in English, German, and Turkish, she offers a global perspective to her contributions in neuroscience</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A35" authindexid="Mosri, Daniela F." listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Daniela</nfirst> <nmid>Flores</nmid> <nlast>Mosri</nlast> <ndeg dgr="PHD"/> <nbio>Psychologist who started her research career investigating sleep disorders at the Reticular Formation Lab (run by neurophysiologist Dr Raúl Alvarado Calvillo) at the National Institute of Neurology and Neurosurgery. Their epidemiological research was awarded second place by the National Council of Psychology (CNEIP) in 2000. Dr Flores Mosri trained as a psychoanalytic psychotherapist and her interest in the dialogue between psychoanalysis and neuroscience began in 1999. With the help of Dr Alvarado, Daniela started studying potential methods to do research in neuropsychoanalysis. She then began her doctoral studies, focusing on addiction and examining the spontaneous neurochemical manipulations by users of psychotoxic drugs as a method of investigating the correlates of neurochemical modifications in affect and psychodynamic features. She has studied borderline pathology from a mainly affective perspective, and is currently conducting research on latent depression. Dr Flores Mosri is a lecturer and researcher at Universidad Intercontinental. She was a member of the National Researchers System (SNI) at the National Council of Science and Technology (CONACyT). Her clinical practice focuses on borderline states, addiction, depression, psychosomatic illness, and sleep and eating disorders, amongst others. Since 2014 Daniela has been a liaison officer in Latin America for the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society. She is also Managing Editor of the journal Neuropsychoanalysis</nbio></aut>
<aut affid="A36" authindexid="Unterrainer, Human-Friedrich" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Human-Friedrich</nfirst> <nlast>Unterrainer</nlast> <nbio>Full professor of process and outcome research at the Faculty of Psychotherapy Science at Sigmund Freud University, Vienna, Austria. As a licensed clinical psychologist/psychotherapist, he worked for many years as a leading therapist in long-term inpatient drug-treatment as well as a university lecturer. In 2011, he founded the Center for Integrative Addiction Research (CIAR), funded by the “Grüner Kreis” [Green circle] society (Austria's largest provider of therapeutic community-based long-term drug treatment), which he still heads today. He is habilitated in three subjects: Psychology, theoretical-experimental (t/e) psychiatry, and religious studies. His habilitation-thesis in the field of t/e psychiatry was on a neuropsychoanalytic topic: “Addiction as an attachment disorder: a neuropsychodynamic perspective.” Research topics are the integration of neuroscientific methods in psychotherapy, addictive disorders, personality and attachment, mindfulness and spirituality as well as clinical outcome studies. To date, he has published over 120 articles and book chapters</nbio></aut>

<aut affid="A41" authindexid="Shalev, Idit" listed="true" role="author"><nfirst>Idit</nfirst> <nlast>Shalev</nlast> <nbio>Co-chair of the Israeli Society for Psychosomatics, an Assistant Professor of Psychology and the Director of the Embodiment and Self-Regulation Lab at Ariel University, Israel. The 23rd Annual Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society, Trieste, Italy, 18–20 July 2024: “When the Body Speaks: Conversion Disorder and Beyond”

The 2024 NPSA Congress that was held in wonderful Trieste showcased a wealth of fascinating presentations from diverse and converging perspectives on the topic of conversion disorder. With each passing year the knowledge generated within the realm of neuropsychoanalysis becomes ever more enriching and relevant. The following assembled collection of research and symposium abstracts from the Congress serves to highlight how this meeting proved to be no exception in this regard. The talks covered both research and clinical content. We are most grateful to all of the presenters who contributed so meaningfully to the success of the Congress. I hope that you as the reader will enjoy this summary and consider contributing to one of our future congresses.

The question of how subjective experiences become embodied is an important one. However, does the question only apply to the unpleasant, pathological side of experience or does it equally apply to the pleasant, fully functioning side of human life? Are we only concerned with reducing unpleasant emotions quantitatively, or do additional qualitatively different and unique psychological states emerge on the pleasant side of otherwise unpleasant emotions that are also part of the healing process? In approaching this question, we compared Ed Diener’s Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS), which was designed as a purely cognitive measure of global life satisfaction, with the Affective Neuroscience Personality Scales 3.1, which provides self-report measures of Panksepp’s six primary emotions (excluding LUST), in two English-speaking samples: a main sample and a holdout validation sample. Our data showed strong negative correlations between higher satisfaction with life and lower FEAR, lower SADNESS/Separation Distress, and positive associations (albeit less strong) between higher satisfaction with life and higher PLAY and SEEKING in both samples. The relationships between the SWLS and at least four of Panksepp’s primary emotions suggests Diener’s SWLS incorporates a strong affective component and is not purely cognitive. In addition, a detailed analysis of the negative correlation between the SWLS and the ANPS 3.1 SADNESS scale provides an insight into the importance of the low arousal end of the SADNESS/Separation Distress brain system and supports a continuum of psychological states from high SADNESS, including loneliness and depression, to the emergence of qualitatively distinct low SADNESS psychological states characterized by social comfort, self-confidence and social strength.

The current Bulletin includes reports from twelve regional groups: Bulgaria, Madrid, Manchester, Mexico City, Lithuania, Liverpool, the Netherlands, New York City, Northern California, Sweden, Tel Aviv, and Turkey. These reports summarize important work done before and after the 23rd Congress of the International Neuropsychoanalysis Society, which took place in Trieste, Italy, in July 2024. Several members of these groups presented papers at the Congress, and it has been interesting to learn about the various thoughts, correlations and research being carried out in the world involving neuropsychoanalytic ideas. The regional group coordinators report that one of their most frequent activities has been the presentation of seminars in person and online, in which topics such as hysteria, psychosomatics and consciousness are highlighted. They have also conducted study group sessions, among which have been seminars featuring Maggie Zellner and Mark Solms, along with local experts in related fields. Several groups have taken on the task of translating books and articles into their native languages, in order to encourage and further disseminate the study of neuropsychoanalysis and provide more people the opportunity to understand and learn about different subjects. A topic of interest in several groups relates to the contributions of neuropsychoanalysis to clinical technique, particularly based on the theories of Freud, Jung, and Panksepp; there are positive reports so far. Group members have applied neuropsychoanalytic ideas in general medicine, pediatrics, oncology, and occupational medicine; to the treatment of trauma, personality disorders, and addiction; to the experience of immigration; and the training of an Olympic Gold Medal swimming champion! This new edition of the Bulletin is an opportunity to learn more about the varied and important topics that our regional groups are studying as we broaden and deepen applications of neuropsychoanalysis in research and clinical practice.

Hessel Boerboom  

Introduction

When Freud wrote On Aphasia in 1891 (Freud, 1891), his subject was linguistics: patients who lost their capacity to use language, to use words. He focused on the neurological aspects in strong disagreement with the localizing mainstream; for Freud, using language involved a “networked” brain. His theory no doubt was influenced by his experience with Anna O, the patient who described her therapy with Breuer as “the talking cure.” We find his concept of the “thing-representation” and the “word-representation” also in his Project (Freud, 1950a (1895)). Freud’s great interest in language also shows in his Psychopathology of everyday life (Freud, 1901) where he gives numerous examples of linguistic parapraxis.

So, from the start, there was a strong relationship between linguistics and psychoanalysis. Within psychoanalysis, this relation can be seen in the work by Lacan and Lorenzer. But linguistics went a separate way. In Linguistics and Psychoanalysis, after a broad tour of linguistic theory, Thomas Paul Bonfiglio proposes his own idea of how language is developed (phylogenetic) and how we acquire it (ontogenetic). In my review, I follow Bonfiglio on his tour and include a lot of the names of the researchers he referenced.

Traveling through Linguistics

Linguistics – the study of language – was, in Freud’s days, philology. Bonfiglio quotes Von Humboldt who described the study of language as “the study of the world history of the thoughts and sensations of humankind in all aspects and all stages of its culture” (p. 9). In the second half of the twentieth century, it became linguistics, an autonomous discipline.

Bonfiglio starts his tour with the work of Bréal, one of the founders of semiotics and teacher of de Saussure. Bréal emphasizes the fact that the language we use does not conform to formal logic; instead, overdetermination is most important. A word can be used literally or metaphorically, can be concrete or abstract. Words can carry contradictory meanings, the meaning depending on the context. This is reminiscent of the ideas on the unconscious in psychoanalysis. Bonfiglio then mentions the work of Kristeva. In her book Language: the unknown – An initiation into linguistics she acknowledges the mutual exclusivity between the psychoanalytical model of language and the model of formal linguistics and then offers a possible reconciliation in the future. It is this that Bonfiglio attempts to do in this book.
