Hessel Boerboom  

Neuropsychoanalysis, as the readers of this journal study and practice it, tries to be a common ground to the various “schools” of psychoanalysis, which grew out of a multitude of single-case studies and the clash of personalities, different cultures, and disparate backgrounds. They all start with the knowledge of Freud’s theories, as he developed them – rich picking grounds to choose from. A sometimes underestimated problem while reading Freud is the translation of his work from German into other languages, because, as we know, the meaning of a text can subtly change in translation.

These two books, recently added to the Routledge Neuropsychoanalysis Series edited by Mark Solms, are good illustrations of that endeavor to find common ground and the strong feelings it elicits.

I read strong feelings in The unconscious in neuroscience and psychoanalysis: On Lacan and Freud by Marco Balzarini. In five chapters, he tries to show the danger to (Lacanian) psychoanalysis from the neurosciences. In his view, neuroscience affirms that “Freud” can be explained with neuropsychoanalysis. This poses, in his opinion, a danger to true psychoanalysis: it may be prohibited! So in this book, he proposes to show how the Freudian/Lacanian unconscious – a central concept in psychoanalysis – differs from the unconscious that neuroscience conceives.

In the first chapter, Balzarini explores the concept of the unconscious in current neuroscience. A smorgasbord of neuroscientific findings is presented and placed in relation to Lacanian thinking. We encounter neuroplasticity of the brain, procedural memory, and the contrasting views of localization versus functionalism in brain research. Drive and motor activity are placed in relation to the Lacanian concept of jouissance. Balzarini criticizes the perspective that language can be seen as information processing, which, in his view, reduces the mind to a machine. The affective consciousness of Solms is discussed, as is the idea that libido is the result of certain chemicals in brain circuits. Then Balzarini takes issue with another Lacanian, John Dall’Aglio. In Balzarini’s view, Dall’Aglio holds that

Lacanian psychoanalysis will benefit from being combined with neuroscience, because it would have a better capacity to participate in the mental health discourse . … it will adapt to the prevailing discourse and will be a therapy like the others, that is, a normal therapy (Balzarini, p. 43).

Hessel Boerboom  

Introduction

Dr. Johnson is a man with a mission: to describe the way society contributes to making people vulnerable to addiction. People ill with addiction are at risk of ruining their lives because they are unable to satisfy their emotional needs in a healthy way and use drugs that can kill them instead. That is the shortest summary of this book. Johnson also gives advice on the treatment of addiction based on neuropsychoanalytical insights. The book is well structured, with many vignettes to illustrate the story. Johnson not only has ample theoretical knowledge, but throughout the book, he also shows his personal involvement and experience. He structures his tale in five parts: (1) the addictive drug industry, (2) how addiction works, (3) treatment, (4) public health solutions, and finally (5) mass psychology. This is neuropsychoanalysis with a sociological twist!

Summary

In Part 1, we are introduced to the addictive drug industry. In four chapters, Johnson exposes the way the state and industry combined have created and sustained an addictive drug industry, wherein some drugs are forbidden while other drugs are promoted, not necessarily based on the harm they can do to the mind and body of their users (and the people close to them). He starts by using nicotine addiction as a theme. Johnson describes that people ill with addiction urgently want the drug, even though they know it is harmful for them. Nicotine sensitizes the SEEKING system, as do cocaine and methamphetamine. In Johnson’s opinion, as SEEKING motivates us to do the things we want to do, activating this system by taking a drug like nicotine or cocaine can make us drug dependent. In a healthy person, SEEKING is tuned to the goals that the other life-sustaining drives have, such as sleeping, drinking, eating, having sex, and looking for relationships. SEEKING controls the other six drives that Panksepp outlined. A well-balanced individual feels strong and confident when the SEEKING drive is activated. If SEEKING is hindered when PANIC/GRIEF or FEAR are active, you seek an easy escape, such as nicotine or cocaine. They activate the SEEKING need, and using the drug changes the internal brain-balance structurally, so dependency is established. The nicotine-industry facilitates addiction by modifying the SEEKING-system.

Jane Abrams and Daniela Mosri

Daniela Mosri

Philadelphia, PA, United States
jabramsdsw@gmail.com

Daniela Mosri  

Social behaviors, primates, reciprocity, cortex

In this article, Testard et al. report on research, employing a novel method intended to create naturalistic conditions for identifying social behaviors, along with their neural signatures, in rhesus macaques. Rather than utilizing controlled experiments requiring the macaques to perform specific tasks, the design allowed subjects although caged, to engage in spontaneous interactions with other macaques. Using ethological analysis, computer vision, and wireless recording technologies, the authors reported findings that suggest broadly distributed coding of social behaviors in the cortex. The social interactions identified included affiliative, aggressive, locomotive, feeding, and grooming between males and females. Reciprocity in grooming was noted and grooming appeared to be calming when the macaques were faced with a threat. The authors suggest that reciprocity is central to building and maintaining strong social bonds that are protective under conditions of stress. Furthermore, their findings suggest that the cortical areas involved in these social behaviors may rely on subcortical regions, and they plan to explore this hypothesis in future research. This could be a possible bridge to Panksepp's contention that subcortical regions are associated with our social instincts and is a hypothesis of particular interest to neuropsychoanalysis.

The Question of Science in Psychoanalysis and in Neuropsychoanalysis: Concepts, Methods, and Case Reports

Jane Abrams , Ross Balchin , Virginia Barry , Rudi Coetzer and Daniela Mosri

Daniela Mosri

dannmos@yahoo.com
http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3126-8344

Daniela Mosri  

Psychoanalysis has long been criticized, arguing that it is a field of knowledge without scientificity. Hence, its main contributions and concepts have frequently been disregarded. This issue of Neuropsychoanalysis not only addresses the topic but also offers rich ideas and research that challenge the latter perspectives. However, neuropsychoanalysis is being questioned as well. The authors that present their work in this issue show how the revision of the most basic pillars of neuropsychoanalysis is part of our ongoing endeavors. We present a collection of articles that cover conceptual, philosophical, and research topics in neuropsychoanalysis that largely advance proposals covering some of the most controversial aspects of psychoanalysis and neuropsychoanalysis, such as the concept of repression, dual-aspect monism, the use of quantitative instruments, and neurological case reports.

Why do we often have very deeply ingrained, immovable opinions, thoughts, or phenomenological experiences? What underpins human bias? Deliberate forgetting, or self-deception? We still need to learn much about this interesting area of human neuroscience. Drawing upon the work of Freud, it has been suggested by several authors that repression could provide a theoretical underpinning for better understanding these phenomena. However, there is not yet a widely accepted, unified theoretical model of repression to better understand these phenomena. In a thought-provoking contribution to this issue, Beate Krickel attempts to address this gap in our knowledge by proposing a unique model of repression in her paper “A Psychological ‘How-Possibly’ Model of Repression” (Krickel, 2024). The author proposes that the “how-possibly” model is a hybrid model, which facilitates overcoming the problems of the higher order and separation models of repression respectively, whilst integrating the strengths into the new proposed model. Krickel’s “how-possibly” model can potentially provide a much-needed theoretical model to inform new research in this area.

Reply to Commentaries - The Separation Distress Hypothesis of Depression - An Update and Systematic Review

Douglas Watt

Douglas Watt

Needham, MA, USA
drdougwatt@gmail.com

New Hampshire, USA

Douglas Watt  

Separation distress, social defeat, depression, evolutionary psychology

A number of very important challenges to the separation distress hypothesis of depression were discussed, clarified, and linked to various strands of existing literature. Foremost among those is the critical challenge to define a more comprehensive set of clinical precipitants, and the possibility that depression may have two prototype elicitors - social defeat and social loss, with hugely overlapping neurobiology, and currently inadequate differentiation in terms of biomarkers and fundamental neurobiology. The possibility of synergism versus exclusionary arguments around about various evolutionary and traditional psychiatric perspectives was advocated. Additional and relevant considerations around mammalian PLAY as an opponent process to depression, and the challenges posed by social constructivist views of emotion were also explored, as these were both neglected in the target article. Social constructivist views and prototype emotion theory are not incompatible; how cognition extensions of prototype ‘elicitors,’ as well as cognized versions of classic prototype affective behaviors might operate is also discussed. There is no way to defend social constructivist views of emotion in animals, and the enormous continuity - from subcortical architectures, neuromodulators and behavioral homologues - argues loudly against any assumption of a fundamental discontinuity between mammalian and human affective endowment.

Primary and Secondary Process Mentation: Two Modes of Acting and Thinking from Freud to Modern Neurosciences

Ariane Bazan

Ariane Bazan

Nancy, France
Ariane.Bazan@univ-lorraine.fr
http://orcid.org/0000-0003-3896-9223

Brussels, Belgique

Ariane Bazan  

Primary and secondary processes, Freud, efference copy, Helmholtz, ventral and dorsal pathways, life and death drives

The purpose of this study is to return to Freud’s original descriptions of the primary and secondary processes in the light of modern neurosciences. In his Project for a Scientific Psychology, Freud draws the axes of the architecture of a mental apparatus: on a horizontal plane, the primary process transfers the excitation by impinging stimuli over a sequence of analogous states towards their discharge; thus, the primary process is essentially characterized by its associative tendency. On a vertical plane, the secondary process opposes the primary bottom-up pressure by a top-down inhibition with its origins in the purposive idea: the secondary process is essentially characterized by its inhibitory interventions. Freud later proposed that the primary and secondary process are seeking for perceptual, respectively thought identity. These different elements are coherent with the dynamics of the ventral and dorsal brain pathways respectively. Moreover, the dorsal pathway has an inhibitory influence upon the ventral pathway, much like the secondary has upon the primary. This influence is exerted thanks to what Freud called the “indications of reality.” We propose to equate these indications with the efference copies in modern neurosciences since they proceed from the same physiology and have the same function, besides originating from the same Helmholtzian source. Finally, even if both primary and secondary processes serve the death drive through the pleasure and the reality principle respectively, only the secondary process, requiring the bearing of an accumulation of excitations, also serves the life drive.

Michelle van den Engh

Michelle van den Engh

Vancouver, Canada
http://orcid.org/0000-0003-1688-8385

Vancouver, Canada
CA 213, Coronation Annex, 1952 Bay Street, Victoria, BC, V8R 1J8, Canada
michelle.vandenengh@ubc.ca

Michelle van den Engh  

Receptivity, neurodiversity, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, neuroscience, predictive coding, mindfulness

Receptivity to our patients’ experience is a vital aspect of the psychoanalytic endeavor. As we receive incoming transmissions, we resonate with what is active in the patient. We hope to then jointly metabolize the experience. When we meet neurodiversity, realms of experience emerge that may elude us. Precipitously formulated ideas in the therapist, based on a neurotypical frame of reference, can impinge upon the discovery of our patients’ authentic world. How do we open ourselves to receive their true experience? This clinical narrative tracks the psychoanalytic travels of an individual who identifies as neurodivergent, who helped the therapist learn to deepen receptivity by dipping into a less differentiated place to follow the here-and-now experience from the bottom up. Throughout the journey, interweaving neuroscientific and psychoanalytic perspectives offered a powerful matrix from which an enriched understanding of our process could emerge. Psychoanalytic concepts including evenly suspended attention, unconscious-to-unconscious communication, alpha function, reverie, and negative capability are explored alongside neuroscientific insights into the stress response, mirror neurons, and the default mode network. A predictive coding lens introduced a view of the therapeutic exchange as a continuous reciprocal prediction, evoking the hypothesis that deepening receptivity required opening awareness to incoming signals and lessening the hold of prior predictions. To bring greater therapist awareness to the present moment and lessen the influence of self-referential evaluation, neuroscientifically-informed reflections also inspired the practice of mindfulness. Subsequent developments suggest that these approaches helped deepen receptivity to the experiences being communicated, leading to new understandings with transformative potential.

A Transcendental Materialist Frame for Neuropsychoanalysis: Rethinking Dual-Aspect Monism

John Dall'Aglio

John Dall'Aglio

211 Rockwell Hall, 600 Forbes Ave, Pittsburgh, PA 15282 USA
dallagliojohn@gmail.com
http://orcid.org/0000-0003-4620-743X

John Dall'Aglio  

Ontology, epistemology, materialism, free energy principle, metaphysics, reductionism

As the philosophical basis for neuropsychoanalysis, dual-aspect monism is fundamental to the entire neuropsychoanalytic project. However, dual-aspect monism has been criticized not only from without but also from within neuropsychoanalysis. This paper considers criticisms of dual-aspect monism from within neuropsychoanalysis. These might be summed up as a concern that the difference at the level of epistemology (neuroscience, psychoanalysis) and phenomena (objectivity, subjectivity) must not be washed away by an appeal to a common ontology. In response, I propose to supplement dual-aspect monism with the philosophical framework of Transcendental Materialism. In this view, epistemological difference between the dual aspects is secondary to antagonism at the level of monistic ontology. Transcendental Materialism begins with the question: what sort of nature must nature be to give rise to two irreducible perspectives such as neuroscience and psychoanalysis? I argue for supplementing dual-aspect monism with Transcendental Materialism through a review of Mark Solms’s work on the hard problem of consciousness via Karl Friston’s Free Energy Principle. Within the Solms-Friston framework, the informatic mechanisms that give rise to dual-aspect epistemologies rely upon ontological antagonism. Principles of a transcendental materialist dual-aspect monism for neuropsychoanalysis are put forward.
